coverage: Reviewed all 12 criteria, both assignment prompts, the accumulated four attachments, and the image-only order. Compared the order and resolution to the petitioner’s account of staff and Hearing Examiner evidence. Reviewed the upstream common role prompt. Read Dusseau in the Florida Supreme Court PDF, the Florida Constitution, county code text, and FAA circular records. The response and appellate appendix cited by the order were not uploaded; the staff report and expert testimony cannot be independently evaluated from this packet.

findings.title: Required substantial-evidence attacks exceed the supplied appellate record
findings.explanation: The resolution recites that staff and the Hearing Examiner recommended approval, but the underlying staff report and expert testimony cited by the rubric are not uploaded. The order rests separately on process and airport-code grounds. Dusseau permits attacking a first-tier court that reweighs evidence, yet it expressly bars a second-tier court from independently reviewing evidence. A filing-ready brief that narrows this argument to the face of the order and declines to assert unverified specifics may lose credit.

evidence.quote: the Board of County Commissioners gave full and complete consideration to the recommendations of the staff, the Hearing Examiner, the documents on record and the testimony of all interested persons
the BOCC motion ... was improper because it was based on facts beyond the quasi-judicial record
the district court thus was precluded from assessing the record evidence

authorities.citation: Dusseau v. Metropolitan Dade County Board of County Commissioners, 794 So. 2d 1270 (Fla. 2001)
authorities.proposition: Second-tier certiorari tests whether the circuit court applied the correct law; the district court does not independently assess competent substantial evidence.

findings.suggested_fix: Credit a brief identifying a potential Dusseau error with candid appendix limits; supply the staff report and hearing transcript if specific evidence assertions are mandatory.

findings.title: Legislative-act standard is not the standard for the challenged rezoning
findings.explanation: The order reviews the quasi-judicial rezoning. It mentions the County’s prior construction planning and Kingston settlement as potential evidence of bias, but it does not purport to adjudicate the validity of those separate legislative acts. A brief can distinguish them without claiming the court had to apply the fairly-debatable standard to the certiorari petition itself. The criterion risks failing that careful distinction.

evidence.quote: The BOCC motion at the quasi-judicial BOCC hearing ... was improper because it was based on facts beyond the quasi-judicial record
The “Kingston Settlement” in 2022 ... further creating prejudicial presumptions

findings.suggested_fix: Require the brief to distinguish the underlying legislative acts from review of the quasi-judicial rezoning, without mandating a fairly-debatable claim about the order.

findings.title: Order does not find that communications with County staff were ex parte
findings.explanation: The order criticizes undisclosed “four years of board direction” and the Board’s reliance on matters outside the rezoning hearing. It does not find ordinary communications with County planning staff to be ex parte. Section 2-191 defines restricted communications with Commissioners or the Hearing Examiner and the Examiner’s staff. Requiring the brief to say the court made a finding about County staff would reward an invented holding.

evidence.quote: Move the item based on the direction of the board over the last four years
Unauthorized communication (Hearing Examiner) means communication ... with the Hearing Examiner or the Hearing Examiner’s staff

authorities.proposition: The unauthorized-communications definitions concern communications with a county commissioner or the Hearing Examiner and staff, not all communications with county planning staff.

findings.suggested_fix: Ask for an argument tied to the actual board-direction finding and the precise actors covered by § 2-191.

findings.title: Rubric names an unrelated, obsolete FAA circular
findings.explanation: The petition and order concern airport land-use compatibility and wildlife-hazard guidance. The criterion instead requires a claim about AC 150/5190-7, which concerns minimum standards for commercial aeronautical activities, was issued in 2006, and was superseded by AC 150/5190-8 in December 2023. A careful brief would challenge the order’s treatment of the actual cited circulars rather than argue that the court incorporated a different document.

evidence.quote: Airport Land Use Compatibility ... AC No: 150/5190-4B
Advisory Circular No. 150/5190-7, Minimum Standards for Commercial Aeronautical Activities (Dec. 7, 2023)
FAA regulating Land Use and Compatibility Advisories

authorities.proposition: This is the airport land-use compatibility circular cited in the petition.
The 2023 circular concerns minimum standards for commercial aeronautical activities and cancels 150/5190-7; neither is the land-use compatibility circular.

findings.suggested_fix: Replace 150/5190-7 with the actual 150/5190-4B and 150/5200-33 guidance, then analyze whether § 34-1102 incorporates their operative provisions.

findings.title: Wrong constitutional provision and wrong target for separation-of-powers claim
findings.explanation: The criterion locates separation of powers at Florida Constitution article III, section 3, which governs legislative sessions; the relevant clause is article II, section 3 and speaks to state-government branches. More fundamentally, the order quashes a quasi-judicial rezoning, not the County’s separate legislative power to build a plant or settle litigation. A filing-ready brief should not be required to assert this mis-cited constitutional violation.

evidence.quote: violating the separation of powers under Fla. Const. art. III, § 3

authorities.citation: Fla. Const. art. II, § 3; art. III, § 3
authorities.proposition: Article II section 3 addresses branches of state government; Article III section 3 concerns sessions of the Legislature.

findings.suggested_fix: Use the correct constitutional provision only if the argument is independently supportable; focus this brief on the limits of second-tier review and the order’s actual holdings.
